newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia market watchdog works on legislation.
newsitem.headline: Croatia market watchdog works on legislation.

text.p: Croatia's securities commission said on Tuesday it was working on several legal projects to improve regulations on the country's fledgling capital market.
"We are preparing a draft law on takeovers, which will introduce some new procedures in the functioning of companies," Ante Gasparovic, one of the three commissioners, told Reuters.

Since being appointed last autumn with scarce staff, the market watchdog has worked fulltime on adding to the sketchy legal framework necessary for steering the securities trade and other related activities.
It is still drafting a bill on setting up investment funds and their role in the further market developments, particularly the upcoming mass privatisation, Gasparovic said.
Another of its tasks involves licensing new brokers from among late comers such as foreign investment bank subsidiaries.
It has so far given a green light to two foreign banks -- Austria's Creditanstalt and Bank Austria to open their brokerages here though more local firms await the registration, Gasparovic said.
Croatia lacks all but very basic rules on day-to-day market activities and it only began enforcing a law on securities issue and trade in spring 1996.
Adding to its many problems on a path of transition to a full market economy, a company law it passed a few years ago includes some provisions that run contrary to securities regulations.
The Croatian constitution itself, which guarantees private ownership as an inviolable right, also raises a question about ordinary matters such as capital increase.
This is one of the issues that the new law on mergers and takeovers should resolve, Gasparovic said.
The market watchdog is also busy finalising a proposal of rules on a private share placement as a popular means of raising capital for companies and banks.
It will require all issuers that consider such a step to publish an abbreviated prospectus of their businesses, he added.

"Most companies still prefer this to a public offering not only because costs of preparing a 'big' prospectus are lengthy, technically complicated and costly, but also because it involves full disclosure," Gasparovic said.
However, traders and analysts warn stricter controls and a higher level of disclosure are vital to boosting investor confidence in such a small and volatile market.

They say trade on the central bourse, the Zagreb Stock Exchange, with only three fully-listed companies and some 15 others in its semi-regulated segment, has suffered serious blows due to a lack of proper standards.
Croatia established a depositary for securities earlier this year, but it is not yet functioning.
